Islands face unique energy challenges, including heavy dependence on imported fossil fuels and workforce limitations, especially the shortage of trained technicians required to maintain new advanced energy assets (NLR 2024a). Additional challenges include the technical difficulties of integrating variable energy generation into small grids, aging generation assets, long lead times for the delivery of specialized equipment, and frequent typhoons (NLR 2024a). For example, some Pacific power utilities have experienced challenges when dispatching solar assets due to inadequate energy storage. The energy infrastructure in this region is particularly vulnerable to severe storms, and the intensity of tropical cyclones is increasing over time (Klotzbach et al. 2022). This exacerbates the need for more backup power and a greater variety of power sources for U.S. bases to ensure uninterrupted power in a region that is critical to the forward posturing of U.S. forces. In Guam, for example, the U.S. Navy accounted for more than 20% of the Guam Power Authority’s energy sales in 2023 (Scarpitti and Voss 2024). When considering small modular reactors as an energy option, sociocultural views might have an impact on acceptability. For example, historical experiences with nuclear weapons, including Hiroshima, Nagasaki, the Fukushima disaster, and mid-20th century nuclear testing in the South Pacific, have contributed to widespread regional aversion to nuclear technologies. This sentiment is reflected in the 1985 South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty, in which signatory nations pledged not to develop or test nuclear weapons (South Pacific Bureau for Economic Co- operation 1987). Although the treaty does not explicitly prohibit nuclear energy generation, the agreement underscores a strong cultural commitment to keeping nuclear activities out of local communities. C.1 Strategic Leadership Strategic competitors, particularly China, are using energy investments to expand their geopolitical influence in the USINDOPACOM region, where control over or cooperation with island nations is key to overcoming geographic challenges. China’s dominance in solar, wind, battery, inverter, and large power transformer technologies and supply chains has made Indo- Pacific nations increasingly reliant on China-supplied infrastructure. Figure C-1 illustrates the growing share of electricity production from solar and wind among countries in USINDOPACOM’s area of responsibility. For example, the Cook Islands’ recent embrace of Chinese infrastructure investment, diplomatic engagement, and strategic alignment highlights how China is leveraging advanced energy technologies as one aspect of a broader strategy to expand its influence in the USINDOPACOM region.
